newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus PM joins fight against Lukashenko vote.
newsitem.headline: Belarus PM joins fight against Lukashenko vote.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko, branded a dictator by a growing political opposition in the former Soviet republic of Belarus, faced mutiny in his usually loyal government on Monday.
Prime Minister Mikhail Chigir met parliamentary leaders who quoted him as saying he would resign unless Lukashenko cancelled a referendum set for Sunday which would significantly boost his powers.

Police stepped up security in the capital as parliament gathered for an emergency session at 2 p.m. (1200 GMT). Around 100 of the 199 deputies were present when the session started, enough to form a quorum but not enough to impeach the president.
The president himself was due to address a rally at the same time in the town of Gomel, near the Ukrainian border.

Interfax news agency quoted him as telling journalists that parliament was trying to put "wild pressure" on the government to resign, but that only the president could decide on the government's fate.
Lukashenko did not refer directly to his prime minister's resignation threat, which was revealed in Minsk by deputy parliamentary speaker Gennady Karpenko.
"Chigir has set the president economic and political conditions, including cancelling the referendum," Karpenko told reporters.
Chigir neither confirmed nor denied he had resigned, saying: "Not so fast, not so fast". But a government official who asked not to be named said Chigir had taken the decision days ago.

The fact that Chigir had met parliament leaders who are united against Lukashenko was a sign he could be changing sides -- potentially a big blow to Lukashenko, who has launched an aggressive campaign to tighten his grip on rival institutions.

Lukashenko named Chigir prime minister after winning a July 1994 election by a landslide, wooing impoverished Belarussians with sensational statements about wiping out top-level corruption and rebuilding a union with neighbouring Russia.
The prime minister is a well-respected figure in the republic of 10 million where Lukashenko already has a rebellious parliament and constitutional court to deal with.
Deputies have been occupying the chamber around the clock since Friday, fearing they could face the same fate as Viktor Gonchar, the man they named as Belarus's top electoral officer.
Lukashenko's security services barred Gonchar from his office and sealed off the Central Commission for Elections and Referendums after Lukashenko sacked him on Thursday.
The country's political struggle has also been reflected on the streets of Minsk, where the latest in a series of protests erupted in clashes with police on Sunday.
A police spokesman said eight people had been arrested and four policemen injured at Sunday's protest. The meeting's organisers said 20 protesters were injured and 10 arrested.
Lukashenko kept up his campaign to muzzle the media late on Sunday, threatening through his Security Council to block broadcasts from neighbouring Russia's NTV television.
"NTV reported fights and bloodshed in Minsk. There was nothing of the kind. The republic's leadership will be forced to take appropriate steps," a Council statement said.

Lukashenko has threatened to deport Russian journalists caught without Belarussian accreditation. Earlier this week he extended the threat to others from further afield, saying: "On November 25 I will also deal with foreign correspondents".
Lukashenko, a former state farm chief, sent postcards to the entire electorate at the weekend with a photograph of his smiling face and appeals to back him.
State-run television broadcasts several advertisements a day urging people to take advantage of early voting which is intended for those who cannot make it on Sunday.

The 42-year-old leader has attracted criticism abroad as well as at home for the referendum, in which he is seeking to extend his term by more than two years, appoint half the commission which monitors elections and half the constitutional court, and to name part of a new, upper house of parliament.
